newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK's Patten grows more credible, Tung less so - poll.
newsitem.headline: HK's Patten grows more credible, Tung less so - poll.

text.p: Hong Kong's outgoing Governor Chris Patten has gained credibility while his successor Tung Chee-hwa has lost some in the six months before the handover of the British colony to China, a poll showed on Sunday.

About 54.2 percent of respondents in a survey conducted by the University of Hong Kong on June 26 said they thought Patten was credible, up from the 46.7 percent in a similar poll in early January, and 40.8 percent in early 1994.

In the same poll this month, 47 percent of respondents thought Tung, picked by a Beijing-supervised caucus late last year to lead the territory after the handover, was credible. That represented a drop from the 63.3 percent in January.
China retakes Hong Kong at midnight on Monday, ending 156 years of British colonial rule.
About 62.5 percent of respondents in the June survey said the sitting legislature was credible, versus 66.3 percent with that opinion in January.
Those percentages compared with 48.3 percent in early 1994, before the chamber became a fully-elected assembly in 1995.

About 19.8 percent of respondents in the latest poll thought a legislature appointed by Beijing to provisionally take over from the present chamber after the handover was credible, a fall from the 22.1 percent recorded in January.

In the June poll, 71.9 percent said news media in Hong Kong were credible, higher than the 59.8 percent that said foreign news media were credible, and 17.7 percent who said news media in China were credible.

About 40.9 percent had a "quite good" or "very good" impression of Hong Kong's British garrison, which will retreat at the handover, and be replaced by the Chinese People's Liberation Army which had left a "quite good" or "very good" impression to 16.6 percent of the respondents.

The June survey polled 546 people with a response rate of 43.1 percent, and the January exercise contacted 599 people with a success rate of 44.7 percent. The 1994 survey polled 1,034 people, of whom 51.7 percent responded.
